newsitem.title: BELGIUM: European Union readies for key Asia meetings.
newsitem.headline: European Union readies for key Asia meetings.

text.p: The European Union embarks on a tightrope walk this week with a series of key meetings with Asian partners that will test the art of diplomacy to the limit.

Foreign ministers from the 15-nation bloc will be in Singapore from Thursday for a meeting with their counterparts from the seven-member Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) before talks with the wider ASEM (Asia-Europe Meeting).
While EU officials are publicly using words such as "routine, friendly and uncontroversial" to predict how they think the meeting will go, privately some admit to misgivings.
"At the back of everyone's mind -- actually, at the front -- are human rights, labour rights and Burma," said one European Commission official involved in planning the meeting.
"How do you speak about the unspeakable? These subjects have to be raised yet no one wants to be the one to do it."
The ASEAN meeting is being heralded as an example of how the EU's links with the organisation are growing.

But at the heart of this growth are differences between Asia and Europe over the enlargement of the organisations -- a subject which will come to the fore when the EU signs an agreement with Vietnam which, in effect, acknowledges Hanoi's recent membership of Asean.
ASEAN -- which now groups Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Philippines, Thailand and Vietnam -- has made no secret of its plans to expand to take in Cambodia, Laos and Burma.

The issue of Burma's membership is particularly vexing as the European Parliament has repeatedly warned the European Commission -- the EU's executive -- that it will not tolerate dealings with Rangoon.
But European leaders, who routinely rebutt Russian complaints over NATO enlargement with the refrain "membership is a matter for members", have drawn short of criticising ASEAN's expansion plans.

"Burma's membership is speculation at this point," said Gwyn Morgan, head of the Commission's department responsible for relations with southeast Asia. "But there is no doubt everyone is aware of the consequences should Burma become a member".

The EU looks as if it might have found a way to mollify the parliament by stressing the letter of its agreements with ASEAN. During a news briefing, Morgan stressed that the EU had an agreement with the "current" membership of ASEAN and any new member -- as in the case of Vietnam -- would have to be the subject of a bilateral agreemnt.

Privately, officials say this means the EU could continue to have relations with an ASEAN which included Burma merely by ignoring the fact. "If you don't have a deal with Burma, it doesn't matter if they are a member or not," said one official
ASEM, which groups the EU and ASEAN with China, Japan and South Korea, also has its eyes on expansion but this too is proving difficult.
Australia and New Zealand have made no secret of their desire to join and appear frustrated by what many of their diplomats view as being excluded by "the Asian element".
Asian nations appear to be sticking to the belief that Asian membership of ASEM is a matter for Asian nations and European membership for the Europeans -- a view disputed by the Commission.

"There is no automacity of membership," said Percy Westerlund, head of the Commission's department responsible for relations with the far east. "New EU members will not necessarily become ASEM members and nor will new ASEAN members," he added.

It is subjects like this that are likely to tax diplomats meeting in Singapore at the end of the week, although they are likely too to stress progress on issues such as certification, customs harmonisation and increased economic cooperation
